items.title: Reject
items.body:
Fixes #429

Serializer.loads currently accepts and ignores arbitrary keyword arguments. This lets URLSafeSerializer silently accept max_age, which only applies to URLSafeTimedSerializer and can hide an incorrect token-expiration configuration. Remove the unused kwargs parameter so unsupported arguments raise TypeError at runtime and are rejected by type checkers. TimedSerializer keeps its explicit max_age API.

Tests: PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/test_itsdangerous/test_serializer.py tests/test_itsdangerous/test_timed.py -q (145 passed); PYTHONPATH=src python -m ruff check src/itsdangerous/serializer.py tests/test_itsdangerous/test_serializer.py; python -m compileall -q src/itsdangerous/serializer.py tests/test_itsdangerous/test_serializer.py.

items.title: AI spam
items.body:
## What this changes and why

### The path problem (primary)

Before this PR, a new user arriving at the itsdangerous docs faced two structural problems that compounded each other:

1. **Wrong toctree order.** The docs listed `serializer` before `signer`, so users read about the higher-level `Serializer` wrapper *before* they had any mental model of the `Signer` primitive it is built on. The conceptual dependency was backwards — you can't reason about what a `Serializer` does for you if you don't yet understand what a `Signer` is.

2. **README dropped users into the most-specific subclass first.** The opening code example used `URLSafeSerializer` with no framing, so the very first mental model a new user built was of a specific, convenience subclass rather than the core abstraction. When they then hit the concepts page — which assumes you understand the `Signer`/`Serializer` distinction — they had no foundation to stand on.

Together, these two issues meant the natural reading order actively worked against understanding.

### What changed structurally

- **Toctree reordered to `signer → serializer`.** The docs now read in dependency order: you learn the primitive first, then the wrapper built on top of it.
- **README gains a 2-sentence framing paragraph** before the code example. Users now know what layer they are looking at before they see code, so the first mental model they build is correct rather than upside-down.

### Copy fixes (secondary)

- **`serializer.rst` — broken import in "Responding to Failure" example.** The example used `URLSafeSerializer` but never imported it, which would raise a `NameError` for anyone who tried to run it. Fixed the import, and added a short note explaining why that specific subclass is used in that section.
- **`timed.rst` — no orientation paragraph.** The page launched straight into API details with no explanation of when to reach for `TimestampSigner` vs `TimedSerializer`. Added a short paragraph so readers understand the choice before they start reading the API.

items.title: timestamp less than zero
items.body:
I've got a bit of a problem that I'm not sure what the best way to resolve it is.  The root seems to be from timed.py with this block of code:

```
if age < 0:
  raise SignatureExpired(
    f"Signature age {age} < 0 seconds",
    payload=value,
    date_signed=self.timestamp_to_datetime(ts_int),
)
```

And that seems to have come about from this issue: https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/issues/126

The reason why I'm running into this problem is because I have multiple servers, all with the same key and salt, they're all able to validate and decode my payload, but every once in a while, the time gets slightly out of sync.  So a user makes a request to server A, immediately makes a request to server B with the same session but the create timestamp is 1-2 seconds into the future.  This causes itsdangerous to label that < 0 which clears my session entirely and logs the user out.

It happens very rarely, maybe once every 6 months but has been extremely difficult to track down.  My planned workaround is to specifically look for this negative age and if it's within what I think is acceptable, go ahead anyway.

Is this something that should be in the package?  Or is there something else I should be doing?  No one else seems to have this problem, so perhaps I'm doing something very wrong.  I'm trying to have a scenario where I could guarantee this isn't possible, but when dealing with two separate servers and a fast enough client it just seems like it _could_ always happen.  My implementation is through a flask application (version 3.1.0) using itsdangerous 2.2.0

Anyone with other suggestions?
